paragraphs.heading: The fissile uranium
paragraphs.text: Uranium-235 makes up about 0.72% of natural uranium. Unlike uranium-238, the main isotope, it is fissile, meaning it can sustain a nuclear chain reaction. It is the only fissile isotope found in nature as a primordial nuclide, and Arthur Jeffrey Dempster discovered it in 1935. Its half-life is 704 million years.

paragraphs.heading: How the chain reaction works
paragraphs.text: Each time a uranium-235 nucleus splits, it releases an average of 2.43 neutrons, most often two or three. If at least one of them hits another nucleus and makes it split, the chain reaction keeps going. A reaction that sustains itself is called critical, and the amount of uranium-235 needed for that is the critical mass. Slowing the neutrons down, called moderating them, makes fission more likely, so a chain reaction can run even at low concentrations of uranium-235.

paragraphs.heading: Slow and fast neutrons
paragraphs.text: For slow thermal neutrons, the fission cross section of uranium-235 is about 584.3 barns, while for fast neutrons it is around 1 barn. Most neutrons it absorbs make it split. A minority, about 15%, turn it into uranium-236 instead.

paragraphs.heading: Fuel for reactors
paragraphs.text: The energy from splitting uranium-235 powers most nuclear reactors and nuclear weapons. Enrichment raises the share of uranium-235 in natural uranium, which is mostly uranium-238. Heavy water reactors and some graphite moderated reactors can run on natural uranium, but light water reactors need low enriched uranium because light water absorbs more neutrons. Highly enriched uranium is sometimes used in the reactors of nuclear submarines and in research reactors. A reactor's power is adjusted by moving control rods that hold strong neutron absorbers such as boron, cadmium or hafnium.

paragraphs.heading: Weapons
paragraphs.text: In a nuclear bomb the reaction is uncontrolled, and the large burst of energy makes a nuclear explosion. The Little Boy bomb dropped on Hiroshima on August 6, 1945, used highly enriched uranium with a large tamper, a layer of dense material around the core that delays its expansion and keeps it supercritical longer. Without a tamper, the nominal critical mass is 56 kilograms, which would be a sphere 17.32 centimetres across. Weapons grade uranium is 85% or more uranium-235, though 20% is enough for a crude, inefficient weapon.

paragraphs.heading: A clock for the galaxy
paragraphs.text: The ratio of uranium-235 to uranium-238 can also be used for dating, measuring the time since these nuclei formed in stars. The 1957 B2FH paper explained the r-process that makes both isotopes, and its authors predicted that r-process events add them in a ²³⁵U/²³⁸U ratio of 1.64. Over billions of years that ratio falls to today's value of 0.0072. In one scenario, a steady series of supernovae over the Milky Way's lifetime, they estimated the galaxy's age at around 10 billion years; the modern value is 13.61 billion years.
